summary: Discovery focused on unit economics across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private; strong interest in using KV cache and batching to hit budgeted $/1000 token targets. Customer is budget constrained for Q1 pilot and wants clear pilot success criteria and security assurances.
transcript:
[00:00] Rob (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Rob from Redwood - joining me are Priya, our solutions engineer, and Samira from customer success. How's everyone?
[00:07] Jamal (Customer): Hey Rob, Leah and Marcus are here, and Rita from finance. We're excited — trying to understand how much this will actually cost us in production.
[00:15] Priya (SE): Quick agenda — we'll run through your current infra, talk unit economics (per-token), batching and KV cache levers, hosting options, and then outline a pilot.
[00:25] Leah (Customer): Nice. We're most worried about runaway token costs — we have a consumer-facing assistant, avg session length ~350 tokens per request, about ~120k requests/day currently. Budget is tight.
[00:36] Rob: Got it. Does that 350 include system + user + model output tokens?
[00:40] Leah: Yeah that's end-to-end. Sometimes we get 600 for longer flows.
[00:44] Priya: Okay. Two levers that usually move the needle: batching and prefix/KV caching. Also model choice and quantization. Are you on a strict regulatory timeline — like do you need private deployment?
[00:54] Marcus: Not in the pilot. We may need VPC or on-prem by mid next year for certain customers, but for now it's about unit cost.
[01:01] Rob: Understood. For Hosted, our per-token list is competitive; dedicated gives reserved throughput and lower per-token when you commit; private is the highest operational overhead but data residency. For numbers, we'll send a detailed spreadsheet.
[01:12] Rita (Finance): Can you ballpark? If we run 120k requests/day x 350 tokens, what are we looking at monthly?
[01:19] Priya: Rough calc: 120k*350 = 42M tokens/day, hmm that's 1.26B tokens/month. If you were on a hosted model at, say, $0.0003 per token (example number), that's... about $378k/month — but batched requests and caching change that.
[01:37] Jamal: Wait that's more than our headcount budget. How much can caching save?
[01:41] Priya: If you can prefix cache common system prompts and a lot of repeated context, we've seen 20-60% token savings depending on repeatability. For a consumer assistant with repeated templates, often low-hanging fruit is 30% without changing UX.
[01:54] Leah: Our prompts are partially templated, but user queries vary. We also do a lot of retrieval augmentation — that increases tokens.
[02:02] Rob: On batching: if you can tolerate a small latency increase, batching across orthogonal requests or micro-batching within a user session can cut per-request overhead. It doesn't reduce generated tokens but reduces model call overhead when amortized — effectively reduces per-token cost.
[02:17] Marcus: Can you explain that — I'm hearing both "reduces per-token" and "doesn't reduce generated tokens" — confused.
[02:21] Priya: Yeah, sorry. It doesn't make the model output shorter. But the serving runtime can pack multiple prompts into one GPU batch, which increases throughput and reduces the compute allocated per token. So your $/1000 tokens can drop because utilization rises. It's a serving-efficiency win.
[02:36] Jamal: So batching is more about throughput efficiency than altering the tokens we bill?
[02:40] Priya: Exactly. Billing at Redwood hosted is per token, but your effective cost per token goes down when throughput utilization improves.
[02:47] Rita: Historically our vendor billed per request too; the predictability was poor. Does Redwood offer committed pricing?
[02:52] Rob: Yes — Dedicated is basically a reserved capacity contract. You commit to an amount of GPU capacity and get a lower effective per-token when compared to pure hosted elastic. We can show committed vs on-demand math in the spreadsheet.
[03:04] Leah: What about KV cache — you said prefix cache. Does that live in customer network or on Redwood side?
[03:10] Priya: For Hosted, KV cache runs in our runtime but we encrypt and can integrate with your KMS for key wrapping. For Private, you run cache in your VPC, full control. There's a middle ground: customer-provisioned cache with Redwood orchestration.
[03:25] Jamal: Encryption is a yes for us. We need KMS and audit logs for compliance.
[03:29] Rob: We have KMS integrations and SOC2. We'll attach the security pack.
[03:32] Marcus: Also curious about fallbacks — if we lose dedicated capacity, can Redwood route to hosted?
[03:37] Priya: Yes, smart routing/fallbacks are standard — you can tier by latency/cost and have automatic fallback to a hosted variant, maybe a quantized model, to stay online. That affects unit econ in edge cases.
[03:48] Rita: If you were to show us 3 scenarios — hosted with aggressive caching, dedicated commit with moderate caching, private minimal caching — could we see runway impact?
[03:57] Rob: Totally. We'll build those scenarios in the sheet. We'll need your prompt set and a token histogram so estimates map to reality.
[04:05] Jamal: We'll push that.
[04:08] Priya: Quick note on quantization — moving to 4-bit inference or optimized kernels can reduce GPU memory and cost per token, but there's a quality tradeoff. We'll include modeled tradeoffs.
[04:19] Leah: Do you run your own kernels or rely on third-party libs? We saw some noise about NVIDIA optimized inference vs open kernels.
[04:25] Priya: Our runtime picks kernels based on model arch and hardware; sometimes we use vendor kernels when they materially help. We also instrument quality regressions in the rollout platform so we can gate quantized variants.
[04:36] Marcus: For the pilot, timeline wise we'd like to start a 6-week pilot in January. Budget for pilot is about $50k. Is that feasible?
[04:45] Rob: A $50k pilot can be scoped — typically we run a constrained throughput pilot and a quality pass, plus limited production routing. Goal is to prove per-token numbers and cache hit rates. We'll map out what we can do in the pilot for that budget.
[04:58] Rita: What's the acceptance criteria for pilot? We need both cost and latency targets.
[05:03] Samira (CSM): Usually pilots have 1) measured token / throughput metrics, 2) cache hit rate baseline, and 3) SLO around p95 latency or equivalent. We'll draft an objective of 20-30% improvement in cost-per-effective-token or demonstrate runway for production.
[05:18] Jamal: Sounds fair. Also want to know how to measure 'effective' tokens when local retrieval adds hundreds of tokens per call.
[05:24] Priya: We'll instrument a per-call breakdown: prompt tokens, retrieval tokens, output tokens, and compute-level cost attribution. Redwood Console gives per-route and token-level breakdowns.
[05:36] Leah: Can console show us token-level cost per route for each model variant?
[05:40] Priya: Yes, you can see per-model/per-route token counts and unit cost, and we annotate cache hit ratios.
[05:46] Marcus: On the security front, SOC2 yes, but we also need data residency for EU customers — can Redwood host in EU?
[05:53] Rob: Yes, we have regions and private deploy options for EU residency. For Private, you can keep everything behind your VPC.
[05:59] Rita: Any hidden fees — egress, storage for cache, etc?
[06:03] Priya: There can be storage for cache and snapshot retention costs, and network egress if you're in a different region. We'll call those out. No surprise pricing otherwise.
[06:12] Jamal: Let's talk technical: are there constraints on batching due to personalization/stateful sessions and KV cache interplay?
[06:19] Priya: Stateful sessions complicate batching, but you can micro-batch within a session or use async batching. For per-user personalization, heavy KV usage can reduce batching opportunities but cache reduces tokens. There's a tradeoff between batching-induced latency and cache-induced token reduction.
[06:33] Leah: So maybe our sweet spot is aggressive prefix cache for common system prompts + moderate batching.
[06:39] Rob: Right. Many customers choose a hybrid: prefix cache to remove repeated system prompt tokens, and 10-20ms added latency for micro-batching to increase throughput on calls where you can tolerate it.
[06:51] Marcus: Let's discuss monitoring: if we enable caching aggressively, how to detect correctness regressions?
[06:57] Samira: We recommend canarying cache changes using Redwood Console eval sets and golden prompt comparisons. If cache changes degrade quality, automated regression alerts trigger.
[07:08] Jamal: That's helpful. For the pilot, we need a realistic benchmark run — ideally a 24-48h load test with our traffic pattern, and then a steady 7-day smoke in production. Can Redwood run that?
[07:18] Priya: Yes, we can schedule a benchmark with a dedicated runway and simulate your traffic shape — we just need the pattern and test prompts.
[07:26] Rob: For next steps: We'll send the pricing + scenarios sheet; Priya will book the performance slot; Jamal will send prompt set and token histogram; Rob will attach SOC2/KMS docs.
[07:37] Leah: One last one — you mentioned fallback to quantized variants; are we liable for decreases in quality at the edge?
[07:43] Priya: We provide routing controls — you define acceptable fallbacks and quality gates. We can also set automatic rollback if metrics drop.
[07:51] Marcus: Great. Any competitors we should be aware of from Redwood perspective?
[07:54] Rob: Customers often compare to Anthropic for higher quality (at higher cost), OpenAI for general availability, and self-hosting/NVIDIA runtimes for on-prem GPU control. We'll include a tradeoff slide.
[08:06] Rita: Thanks. We'll review the sheet once received.
[08:09] Rob: Awesome. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and schedule.
[08:13] Jamal: Thanks, bye.
notes: Transcript contains occasional mis-hearings typical of auto transcribe: e.g., 'K-V cash' instead of 'KV cache' and 'Redwood Ded' occasionally. Customer is green to a Jan pilot if budget is scoped.
